quote: people do much better when discussing whether torture is good or bad than when they discuss the meaning of
content: This is presented as "a general syndrome" on the strength of one introspective postmortem of the author's own past reasoning. No measure of "doing better" is offered, and none could be applied without the meta-level standard the sentence is recommending against. The policy is also abandoned immediately: the eleven essays of the Value Theory sequence that follow this one are meta-level from beginning to end, arguing about what "right" refers to, whether moral terms are one-place or two-place predicates, and what a moral computation is. Either the meta level is worse than useless, in which case the next sequence should not exist, or it is where the work of this book actually happens.

quote: people will pay only 28% more to protect all 57 wilderness areas in Ontario than one area, people will pay the same amount to save 50,000 lives as 5,000 lives
content: Both halves of this recollection are inaccurate, and the first is a splice of two different studies described correctly three essays earlier: the 57 wilderness areas were in four western US states (McFadden and Leonard), while the Ontario result was about polluted lakes and came from Kahneman. The second half — equal payment for 50,000 and 5,000 lives — corresponds to no study cited anywhere in this book; the actual lives-based findings are Carson and Mitchell's fourfold increase across a 600-fold risk change and Baron and Greene's null across a tenfold change. An essay whose thesis is that people should attend to quantities rather than to prototypes is here reciting quantities from memory and getting them wrong. The underlying phenomenon is real; this sentence is the prototype of it.

quote: Contributions to individual group members far outweighed the contributions to the entire group.
content: The Israeli psychologists are Kogut and Ritov, and their own papers report the finding with a condition Slovic's popular summary drops: the singularity effect appears in separate evaluation and largely vanishes in joint evaluation, where subjects who see the single child and the group of eight side by side give more to the group ("The Singularity Effect of Identified Victims in Separate and Joint Evaluations," OBHDP 97, 2005). So the correct summary is not that the brain cannot multiply by eight but that the brain does not multiply when it is shown only one option and asked how it feels. That is a real and important limitation, but it makes the failure a property of the elicitation, and the decisions this essay cares about — how to allocate a fixed budget among named alternatives — are joint evaluations. The essay sources the study to a Foreign Policy article rather than to either primary paper, and inherits the summary's missing condition.

quote: if you try to violate “utilitarianism,” you run into paradoxes, contradictions, circular preferences
content: Utilitarianism is not the fixed point where the paradoxes stop. Aggregating welfare additively generates the Repugnant Conclusion, the Mere Addition Paradox, and the Sadistic Conclusion, and Arrhenius's impossibility theorems in population ethics prove that no theory can satisfy a small set of individually plausible adequacy conditions — meaning that the paradoxes are not an artifact of the alternatives but a feature of the whole terrain. The same is true of decision theory once the sums get large: Pascal's Mugging, the St. Petersburg game, and Pasadena-style non-convergent lotteries are all problems for expected-value maximization specifically, and the author would go on to name the first of these himself. "My view has no paradoxes and yours does" is the sort of claim the book elsewhere teaches readers to check.

quote: Three lives are one and one and one. No matter how many billions are doing better, or doing worse.
content: This states separability, which is a substantive axiom in the theory of value, not an arithmetical truth. Every distribution-sensitive view — prioritarianism, egalitarianism, sufficientarianism — denies exactly this: on those views the moral weight of a benefit depends on how well off the recipient is, and therefore on facts about the rest of the population, and none of them is committed to any inconsistency in arithmetic. The deeper gap is that decision-theoretic coherence arguments constrain a single agent's preferences over lotteries and say nothing about summing welfare across persons; getting from one to the other requires Harsanyi's aggregation theorem plus interpersonally comparable cardinal utilities, an addition Sen and Weymark argued smuggles in the ethics it claims to derive. Writing the claim as "3 = 1 + 1 + 1" makes an assumption look like a proof.

quote: As Peter Norvig once pointed out, if Asimov’s robots had strict priority for the First Law of Robotics
content: The argument shows that a strict lexical priority over a domain where the higher-tier value is always slightly in play makes the lower tiers idle — which is a good point against infinite value, and not the same point as the one being made. Threshold deontology, satisficing constraints, and lexical orderings restricted to specified choice types all avoid it while remaining non-aggregative in the disputed cases. The Asimov example also cuts the other way once looked at: nearly every robot story in the corpus turns on the Laws conflicting, being defeated by uncertainty about what constitutes harm, or being satisfied in a way that horrifies everyone, which is Asimov's own demonstration that a lexically ordered rule set does not determine behaviour without an enormous amount of undischarged interpretation. That difficulty does not go away when the rules are replaced by a utility function.

quote: It is a general principle that Bayesians see no difference between the long-run answer and the short-run answer
content: True for expectations, and the essay is entitled to it, but the intuition pump is carrying more than the theorem does. Averaging arguments licence expected-value maximization for repeated small stakes with independent draws; for one-shot decisions over very large or unbounded quantities they fail, which is why Savage's and Fishburn's representation theorems require utility to be bounded for expected utility to be well defined over all lotteries. That requirement is in direct tension with this book's aggregation arguments: a googolplex of hiccups outweighing a torture, and a tiny probability of astronomically large value outweighing certainties, both need unbounded additive utility, and unbounded utility reintroduces the St. Petersburg and Pascal's-Mugging failures the coherence theorems were invoked to avoid. The essay is drawing on two frameworks that cannot both be had in full.
